summary:
Luxembourg imports 95% of its fruits and vegetables. Madagascar loses entire harvests to every cyclone. Existing tools are either too generic (a weather app) or black boxes.

We built TerraLux AI: a decision-support system that fuses 30 years of NASA satellite data (POWER), soil properties (SoilGrids), cyclone history (IBTrACS), and photo-based leaf diagnosis. For any plot on Earth, it delivers a Top 3 crop recommendation with full justification ("pH 6.2 ideal, rainfall 842mm in optimum, rotation respected"), a soil richness index (0-100) at three depths, and a contextual disease risk that cross-checks image diagnosis with real-time climate conditions.

But our true innovation is the Resilience Passport: a certified, timestamped PDF with SHA-256 hash and QR verification that banks can use to assess agricultural loans, insurers to calculate premiums, and governments to target subsidies. No such standard exists.

We address the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge by turning NASA Earth observations into a bankable trust infrastructure. We tested on two climates: Luxembourg (temperate) and Madagascar's Diana region (tropical dry). Our engine recommends rice, cassava, and maize in Antsiranana — exactly the dominant crops — and wheat, potato, and rapeseed in Luxembourg City.

Why it matters: We don't sell an app. We certify resilience. And we propose that Luxembourg become the first country in the world to do it.
